How do you prove to yourself that Bayes’ theorem actually works in the real world—and not just on a blackboard? You **simulate 100,000 virtual worlds in Python**, filter down to the worlds that produced the exact data you observed, and count what fraction came from each hypothesis! **Lab 2** pairs **Monte Carlo simulation** with **sequential Bayesian updating**, showing that simulated frequencies converge straight onto exact analytical Bayes’ rule.

---

## Background Knowledge Map: Core Lab 2 Skills — Monte Carlo Simulation & Sequential Updates

1. **Forward Generative Simulation:** Drawing hidden states $$H^{(s)} \sim P(H)$$ and then data $$D^{(s)} \sim P(D\mid H^{(s)})$$ creates an empirical joint distribution without writing a single integral!
2. **Rejection / Conditioning by Filtering:** Keeping only simulated worlds where $$D^{(s)} == d_{\text{obs}}$$ directly approximates $$P(H \mid D = d_{\text{obs}})$$—the exact conceptual ancestor of Approximate Bayesian Computation (ABC)!
3. **Sequential Updating Invariance:** Updating a posterior one observation at a time matches batch updating on all observations simultaneously.

---



---

### Worked Numerical Example: Verifying Rejection Conditioning Against Exact Bayes

Using the Lab 1 fixture (`P(H1)=0.2, P(E|H1)=0.9, P(E|H2)=0.3`) across $$S = 10{,}000$$ simulated worlds:
- Expected worlds with `(H1, E)`: $$10{,}000 \times 0.2 \times 0.9 = \mathbf{1{,}800}$$.
- Expected worlds with `(H2, E)`: $$10{,}000 \times 0.8 \times 0.3 = \mathbf{2{,}400}$$.
- Filtering to `E` leaves $$\approx 4{,}200$$ worlds, of which $$\frac{1{,}800}{4{,}200} = \mathbf{42.86\%}$$ came from `H1`—matching exact Bayes ($$3/7$$) with Monte Carlo SE $$\sqrt{\frac{0.429 \times 0.571}{4200}} \approx 0.76\%$$!

### Deep-Dive Explanation: Three Lab 2 Verification Habits (Read Slowly)

1. **Check the surviving sample count after filtering:** If only 15 simulated worlds match rare evidence `E`, your Monte Carlo SE is $$\sim 13\%$$—increase $$S$$ to 100,000+ or compute analytically!
2. **Plot the running posterior trajectory after each new data point:** Watching the belief curve smoothly sharpen from observation 1 to observation 50 builds deep intuition for sequential learning.
3. **Verify batch vs. sequential equality:** Assert that updating on `[1, 0, 1]` one step at a time gives the exact same posterior as updating on `k=2, n=3` at once.

**Quick check.** In the $$S = 10{,}000$$ simulation above, why does filtering to `E` discard roughly $$58\%$$ of all simulated worlds?

- [What is Monte Carlo Simulation?](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7TqhmX92P6U) — IBM Technology, English. Watch Monte Carlo generate many scenarios from one assumption; it supports the part of the lab that uses simulation instead of closed-form integrals.
- [Bayes theorem, the geometry of changing beliefs](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HZGCoVF3YvM) — 3Blue1Brown, English. Watch the prior multiplied by the likelihood and then normalized; use it as a map for the update loop in the lab.
